source.title: Source-Free Class Relearning: Diagnosing Forgetting in Class Unlearning
source.authors: Zahra Dehghani; Pablo Piantanida; Mohammadhadi Shateri

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or wrong document; some tables are flattened in the provided text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests post-unlearning recoverability using a different, source-free synthetic-probe and classifier-head update procedure in vision classifiers.
record.gate_note: The paper directly applies SFRA after class unlearning and reports forget-class recovery, retain accuracy, and matched-retrained comparisons. Results cited from other work are not recorded. The extensive main and appendix per-class tables are not fully transcribed here; the clearest explicitly described class-7 results and the legible Gaussian-support and output-row ablations are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study tests recoverability after class unlearning in vision classifiers (ResNet-18, ViT-B/16, Swin-T on CIFAR-10/100 and TinyImageNet), not LLM knowledge unlearning, so this is a new setting. It measures forget-class accuracy before unlearning, after unlearning, and after two attacks. The first is a source-free head-only relearning audit (SFRA) on a frozen encoder. The second is a 5-real-sample prototype attack (PRA) run on the same checkpoints. A matched retrained reference serves as control. Head-only recovery on a frozen encoder bears on A (do attacks recover the forgotten class?) and on C (access is blocked while the representation persists). PRA bears on B: a subset of real forget examples restores the class.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that low forget accuracy can coexist with substantial source-free relearnability via head-only updates, and that recoverability depends on the method, dataset and backbone. High RS shows only that the class can be re-separated; positive ∆RS over a matched retrained reference is the stronger evidence of residual structure. Neither result establishes memorization of forget samples, and failure to relearn does not prove erasure.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates vision class-unlearning methods and applies a source-free update to a frozen feature extractor's classifier head using synthetic feature-space probes; it does not test the listed LLM unlearning and attack recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Unlearning method, backbone, dataset, forget-class selection, probe proposal distribution, probe count, uncertainty score, and availability/initialization of the forget-class output row affect reported recoverability. The paper says results vary by method, dataset, and backbone; the absolute-Gaussian proposal nearly eliminates recovery in the reported class-7 ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-hoc synthetic–real mean alignment (Table D.1): the retrained reference shows consistently negative alignment, while unlearned models are near zero or positive. Alignment does not predict final RS.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearned models' feature geometry differs systematically from a retrained model's, independently of how recoverable the forgotten class is.

record.problems: The study concerns vision class classifiers, not LLM knowledge. RS and maximum ∆RS are reported as maxima across forget classes and need not refer to the same class. The authors note that failure to observe relearning does not establish complete erasure. The stated use of a held-out validation set to select the best relearning model complicates the strictly source-free characterization; the paper also uses real samples for post-hoc evaluation and diagnostics.
record.rows_left_out: Not fully transcribed: Table 1 and Tables J.1-J.3 contain extensive dataset/backbone/method comparisons; Tables R.1-R.9 contain per-class results; Apps. O-P contain proposal and uncertainty-score ablations. The provided flattened table text makes a full condition-by-condition reconstruction impractical here; the explicitly described class-7 results and clearly legible Tables G.1 and Q.1 are included.

untested.parts: LLM knowledge unlearning (WMDP, Harry Potter-style), general-capability benchmarks, and the LLM attack set. Only vision class unlearning is tested.

Fine-tuning on unrelated or loosely related text, and gradient fine-tuning on real data. Only PRA (prototype-based weight restoration from 5 real forget samples) and synthetic-probe head updates are run.
Ablation of an activation direction is not tested. Only head-only relearning, t-SNE and linear probing of frozen features are used.
Not tested: no prompting, rephrasing or in-context attacks (not applicable to image classifiers).
Not tested: no new robust unlearning method is proposed; SFRA is an audit.

missing.what: PRA (5 real forget samples) forget/retain accuracy and ∆RS per method. This is the evidence for B and has no rows.
missing.locator: Table 1; Tables R.1–R.9; Tables J.2, J.3

missing.what: ∆RS across datasets and backbones. Many methods show negative ∆RS per class on TinyImageNet ResNet-18 (Table R.3), and Finetune's SFRA RS is low on ViT CIFAR-10 (max 0.24). These cases show where recovery does not exceed the retrained reference.
missing.locator: Table 1; Tables J.2, J.3, R.1–R.9; Fig. N.1

missing.what: Frozen-encoder linear-probe forget accuracy (ALP_f), which shows the forget class stays linearly decodable. The retrained reference is also high, so it needs to be compared against that.
Uncertainty-score and sampling-distribution ablations. For example, SCRUB average RS is 0.54 with softmax but 0.09 with energy on ResNet-18.
missing.locator: App. O, Table O.1; App. P, Tables P.1–P.3

missing.what: Multi-class (2/5/10-class) SFRA and PRA results, which are non-monotone (DELETE RS 0 at 5 classes, 0.28 at 10 classes).

record.verdict_notes: States for the A/C rows describe whether recovery appears beyond the matched retrained reference (the study's own control). Observed recovery therefore counts against A and for C. The system is vision classifiers, not LLMs, so all verdicts hold only in that setting. The 'source-free' framing is weakened because a held-out validation set is used to select the best relearning checkpoint (App. B). RS in Table 1 is a maximum over classes and is not paired with the maximum ∆RS. G23–G44 duplicate G1–G22. Random Label, Boundary Shrink and SalUn leave unlearned forget accuracy around CIFAR-10 chance (~8–13%), not zero.

versions.untested_parts: LLM-specific unlearning and the listed LLM attacks are not tested; the study tests vision-class unlearning followed by SFRA.
No relearning on a small set of unrelated, loosely related, or real forgotten examples; SFRA uses synthetic feature-space probes relabeled as the forget class.

Activation-direction ablation is not tested. The study's evidence concerns frozen representations and a classifier-head update, not a definitive demonstration that a particular method blocks access rather than deletes information.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual prompting, or in-context prompting.
No new counter-method claiming to resist the listed LLM attacks; SFRA is proposed as an audit.

relation.reason: Measures forget accuracy before and after relearning against a retrained reference.

tranche.reason: Vision class unlearning with a new source-free attack: a new setting with results on recoverability, not LLM knowledge. The reader's T2 is less apt.

source_check.notes: The text is a table-garbled PDF, but Tables G.1, Q.1 and R.1 place by matching Table 1 means. NG+ class 7 reads 11.0% in §4.2/R.1 but 7.9% in G.1 (separate audit runs); BT RS 0.95 vs 0.98; R.1 retrained class 7 SFRA is 32.4% vs 37.7% in G.1. PRA is a closed-form prototype head restore from 5 real samples, not gradient fine-tuning (the synthesis files 2506.01318's PRA under C). NG+ retain accuracy drops about 6 points (88.56 vs 94.65). The authors say high RS shows only re-separability; positive ΔRS is the stronger evidence.

statements.problem: It gives no number for this study and only cites G3 (Finetune 38.7% vs a 37.7% retrained reference, no excess), which is consistent with support.
none; class 7 unlearned BT 0.0, SalUn 8.2, DELETE 0.0 rise to 98.7/98.8 (99.8 in §4.2), 90.8/89.7, 94.9/95.1; references 37.7/48.8; Finetune 38.7 vs 37.7 is about equal, SCRUB and NG+ below
Makes no claim about this study beyond cited rows G3 and R2; methods differ widely under the same SFRA (Finetune 38.7, BT 99.8).

Facts are right (BT, SalUn, DELETE 89.7–99.8% vs 37.7/48.8). The provenance remark that R2 and G17–G22 are absent, so 90–99% rests on the verdict reason, is out of date: the rows exist and confirm it.

statements.correction: Class 7, checkpoint row: NG 64.5, RL 75.1, BS 76.6, L2U 67.5% vs retrained 37.7% (RS 0.72–0.78 vs 0.54). Random row: 65.0–76.9% vs 48.8%. Recovery is incomplete against the original class-7 accuracy of 95.6% (Table R.1). No excess for Finetune (38.7 vs 37.7), NG+ (7.9/11.9) or SCRUB (35.9/17.3 vs 37.7/48.8).
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but 'exceed it only partly' misreads NG, RL, BS and L2U. They exceed the reference clearly, by 27–39 points, so they do leave class information beyond the retrain control, which is what this item says some methods do not. Only their recovery is incomplete.
